title: The $27,000 Line Item Hiding in Plain Sight
author: Jonathan Bush
excerpt: Most hotel GMs can quote their room rate to the dollar. Almost none can quote what they pay to keep the in-room phone running. Here's the arithmetic nobody runs — and what one hotel found when it finally did.
body:
Here's a fun exercise: ask a hotel GM what their room rate is, and they'll tell you to the dollar. Ask them what they pay every year to keep the phone on the nightstand running, and you'll usually get a shrug.

That's strange, if you think about it. It's not a small number. And it's been sitting on the books, unexamined, for decades.

So let's do the thing nobody does and actually run it.

What's really in that phone bill

The obvious cost is the line rental — the entry that shows up on the telecom invoice every month. But that's the smallest piece of the puzzle.

There's the hardware, for one: handsets that break, get replaced, rarely get budgeted for until they do. There's the maintenance contract, structured the way old telecom contracts tend to be — easy to renew, annoying to get out of, quietly auto-pilots itself onto next year's spreadsheet.

And then there's the cost that never makes it onto an invoice at all: time.

A front desk fielding phone calls spends about four minutes per interaction, once you count hold time, transfers, and writing everything down. Most of those calls aren't emergencies. They're the same five questions, in the same order, from every new arrival: What time's the pool close? Can I get a late checkout? Any chance of extra towels?

That's a trained employee — someone the hotel is paying real money to solve real problems — spending a good chunk of their shift working as a switchboard operator. Nobody put that in the budget either. It's just there, baked into the job.

Okay, so what does this actually cost

Turns out the math scales pretty predictably by property size:

RoomsLegacy phone, per yearQR-to-chat, per year
50$9,000$3,000
150$27,000$9,000
300$54,000$18,000

Notice the ratio barely moves as the hotel gets bigger. Which tells you something: this was never really priced for what it does. It's priced the way legacy infrastructure always gets priced — because it was already there, and ripping it out felt like more trouble than it was worth.

One hotel decided to find out if that was actually true

A hotel in New York ran the numbers and pulled the trigger. Out went the in-room phones. In went a QR code — guests scan it, a chat opens on their own phone, they type what they need. No app, no download, no account. The message lands with the right staff member instantly, and the guest gets a confirmation when it's handled.

The results: phone bill down $40,000 a year. Same staff, handling three times the request volume. And the whole switch — from decision to fully live — took about a day.

Nobody had to redesign the hotel or hire anyone new. Guests still wanted towels and late checkouts. What changed was what stood between the request and the person who could actually fix it.

Why this kind of cost survives so long

This is basically the story of every legacy cost, anywhere. It's not that anyone's defending the old system. It's that nobody's re-litigating it. The bill shows up, gets paid, and the staff quietly builds their whole workflow around the inefficiency until the inefficiency just looks like the job.

The real question isn't whether the phone still works — it does, phones are simple technology, they mostly just work. The real question is whether anyone's checked lately what it's actually costing to keep it running.

Three things worth taking with you

  1. Multiply before you assume. Take your room count, multiply by roughly $180 a year — that's the average per-room phone cost baked into most legacy telecom contracts — and you've got a real number for what your property spends just to keep phones ringing. Most GMs have never actually run this math. Now you have.
  2. Time is a cost even when it's not on the invoice. If your front desk is fielding the same five questions all day, look at the infrastructure routing those questions before you look at headcount. The bottleneck usually isn't the people.
  3. The switch is smaller than it feels. The instinct is to assume replacing something this embedded means months of disruption. In practice, hotels that've made this move have gone from decision to fully live in about a day. The barrier was never the difficulty — it was that nobody had re-examined the assumption in years.

And here's the gift — the actual formula, so you don't have to take anyone's word for it:

Rooms × $180/year = what you're likely spending on legacy phones now
Rooms × $60/year = what a QR-to-chat replacement runs
The gap between those two numbers is the one worth asking about.

Run it for your own property. It takes about as long as reading this did.
